procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 07.05.2019 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench in CRLA No.106 of 2000, which upheld the conviction and sentence passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Barabanki in Sessions Trial No.85 of 1996 for offenses under Sections 302 and 307 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal Code, 1860.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The appellant was convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Barabanki in Sessions Trial No.85 of 1996.
2. The appellant filed Criminal Appeal No. 106 of 2000 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, challenging the conviction and sentence.
3. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence in its order dated 07.05.2019.
4. The appellant had also filed a Criminal Revision before the High Court against an order dated 21.08.1999 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Barabanki. The High Court dismissed this criminal revision on 16.09.1999 because the trial was almost complete.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture:
1. The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court upheld his conviction and sentence.
2. The appellant raised a plea of juvenility, predicated on a transfer certificate, which was sought to be relied upon as an additional document before the High Court.
3. The Supreme Court passed an order on 08.10.2021 directing the Trial Court to submit a fresh report on the plea of juvenility raised by the appellant, after appreciating the additional evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a juvenile at the time of commission of the offence.

facts: The appellant claimed to be a juvenile at the time of the offense, which occurred on 01.12.1995.
The plea of juvenility was raised at the trial stage but was dismissed by both the Trial Court and the High Court.
The appellant presented a Scholar Register from his college that recorded his date of birth as 05.07.1980, which would make him 15 years and 6 months old at the time of the offense.
Contradictory evidence was presented in the form of a Family Register from the Gram Panchayat, which recorded his year of birth as 1975, making him approximately 20 years old.
The Supreme Court ordered an inquiry, and a final report from the Additional Sessions Judge, Barabanki, dated 28.09.2022, concluded that the appellant was indeed a juvenile at the time of the crime.
law: The relevant law at the time of the offense was the Juvenile Justice Act, 1986.
Under the 1986 Act, a male was considered a juvenile if he had not completed the age of 16 years.

The Court also noted a legal principle (from Rule 12(3)(b) of the Juvenile Justice Rules) that in cases of conflicting reports and documents regarding age, the court should give the accused the benefit of one year.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged the conflicting evidence regarding the appellant's age (the Scholar Register vs. the Family Register).
The Court chose to rely on the final report submitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Barabanki, dated 28.09.2022, which accepted the appellant's claim.
The Court's decision was further supported by the principle that in cases of conflicting evidence, the benefit of the doubt should be given to the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the final report of the Additional Sessions Judge and declared that the appellant was a juvenile on the date the offense was committed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a juvenile at the time of commission of the offence.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred by not considering the appellant's application (CM No.96164/2012) to submit a transfer certificate as additional evidence to support the plea of juvenility.
This transfer certificate shows the appellant's date of birth as 05.07.1980, which would establish their juvenility at the time of the offence.
The Trial Court had questioned the veracity of the Scholar Register because it was based on this transfer certificate, which was not on record at the time.
The application to place this crucial document on record was filed before the High Court but was never dealt with or decided upon.
respondent_arguments: The plea of juvenility was not raised in the original grounds of appeal before the High Court.
Other documents on record undisputedly show the appellant's age as more than 16 years, contradicting the claim of juvenility.

statutes.act_name: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Rules, 2007
The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000

cases.case_name: Satya Deo alias Bhoorey v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: To explain the impact of Section 25 of the 2015 Act, establishing that the expression 'all proceedings' includes not only the trial but also revision or appeal, which determines the applicability of the relevant rules to pending proceedings.

cases.case_name: Hariram v. State of Rajasthan and Another
cases.principle: To support the principle that the question of juvenility can be examined in pending proceedings, including appeals.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A claim of juvenility can be raised before any court at any stage, even after the final disposal of the case. If juvenility is established, any sentence passed by a court shall be deemed to have no effect, and the case must be referred to the Juvenile Justice Board for passing an appropriate order.
obiter: Where two views on the age of the accused are possible, a liberal view should be taken to extend the benefit of juvenility.
Actions taken or orders issued under the provisions of the Rules of 2007, if not inconsistent with the new rules, are deemed to have been taken or issued under the new rules.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court sustained the appellant's conviction but quashed the sentence. The conviction was upheld because the evidence and the role assigned to the appellant were identical to that of the other co-accused, making it impossible to take a different view on his guilt. However, having been declared a juvenile, the sentences awarded were quashed as they cannot be imposed on a juvenile under Section 16 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000.
legal_tests_applied: If two views are possible on the same evidence, the court should lean in favour of holding the accused to be a juvenile in borderline cases.
A hypertechnical approach should not be adopted while appreciating the evidence adduced on behalf of the accused in support of the plea that he was a juvenile.
Under Section 16 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, certain sentences cannot be given to a person found to be a juvenile.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant lost on the issue of conviction because the evidence against him was common with the other two co-accused, and his role was identical. The Court reasoned: 'The role assigned to the present appellant is no diﬀ erent than the role assigned to the other two accused who were convicted... It is exactly the same role and clearly section 34 of the Indian Penal Code is also attracted. It is not possible therefore to take a diﬀ erent view for the present appellant than what has been taken by the Trial Court and the Appellate court against the other two accused regarding their conviction.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in having the conviction sustained because the Court found that the evidence proving the appellant's guilt was inseparable from the evidence against the other convicted co-accused. The Court determined that since the role played by the appellant was exactly the same as the others, and the evidence was common, the finding of guilt by the lower courts had to be upheld.
policy_considerations: The benefit of the Juvenile Justice Act should be extended to the juvenile in conflict with law, especially in borderline cases where two views on the evidence are possible.
Courts must ensure that the Juvenile Justice Act is not misused by individuals to escape punishment after committing serious offences.
